pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** How fossils form

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Science, Year 3 Rocks):** Pupils describe in simple terms how fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock.

- **Standards — US (NGSS supports 4-ESS1-1 fossils-as-evidence strand):** Describe the basic fossilisation process and recognise common fossil types.

- **Operational details:** This is a sequential PROCESS concept. The child must order the steps: an organism dies → it is quickly buried in mud/sand/sediment → more layers pile on top and press down → over millions of years the sediment turns to rock and minerals preserve the shape → much later the rock is exposed and the fossil found. Two big ideas carry weight: (1) burial must be QUICK before the body rots/scatters, and (2) fossilisation takes an enormous amount of TIME. Distinguish body fossils (shells, bones — the shape preserved in stone) from trace fossils (footprints, imprints — evidence of activity). Teach as an ordered story with strong imagery, linking to prior rock work (fossils are found in sedimentary rock) and prior living/dead work (only once-living things fossilise).
bestPractices: Teach fossilisation as an ORDERED sequence (die → bury → layers build → turn to rock → exposed/found) and have children retell it in order.
Foreground the two big ideas: quick burial (before decay) and immense time (millions of years).
Distinguish body fossils (shape preserved: shells, bones) from trace fossils (footprints, imprints) with examples.
Link to prior learning — fossils form in sedimentary rock, and only once-living things fossilise.
Use vivid before/after imagery and, ideally, a hands-on 'cast' model (plaster over a shell) to make preservation-of-shape concrete.
keyRepresentations: Cross-section showing an organism buried under accumulating sediment layers.
Body-fossil vs trace-fossil example cards (shell/bone vs footprint/imprint).
A cast/mould demonstration (press a shell into clay, fill with plaster).
commonMisconceptions: 'Fossils are the actual bones/animal, unchanged' — not knowing minerals replace/preserve the shape in rock.
'Fossils form quickly' — missing the millions-of-years timescale.
'Any dead thing becomes a fossil' — not realising it needs quick burial and the right conditions (most don't fossilise).
'Fossils are found in any rock' — rather than mainly sedimentary rock.
'A footprint isn't a fossil' — not recognising trace fossils.
'Dinosaurs and fossils are the same thing' — conflating one example with the whole concept.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8, teach how fossils form as an ordered process story: an organism dies, is quickly buried in sediment, more layers pile on and press down, over millions of years sediment turns to rock while the organism's shape is preserved (often as minerals replace the material), and much later the rock is exposed and the fossil found. Two big ideas carry the most weight: burial must be QUICK (before the body rots or scatters) and fossilisation takes an ENORMOUS amount of time. Distinguish body fossils (shells, bones — shape preserved in stone) from trace fossils (footprints, imprints — evidence of activity). Link to prior learning that fossils occur mainly in sedimentary rock and that only once-living things fossilise. A driveable simulation of the process is proposed as the central activity, with sequencing/sorting practice, a retelling task, a tap-to-reveal cross-section, an optional excavation and expert Q&A, and a hands-on plaster-cast as complements. These are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

activities.title: Fossil-formation time machine (drive the process)
feedback: If the learner waits instead of burying quickly: show what fits the chosen specimen — soft parts rotting and being eaten, or a shell or bones being broken up and scattered by animals and water — then prompt — 'Nothing was left to preserve. Why do you think burial has to happen fast?'
At the time slider, reinforce: 'Notice how far you had to sweep — this takes a very long time, millions of years, not days or weeks.'

When the fossil is excavated, confirm the shape was kept while the material was often slowly replaced or turned to rock: 'The rock kept the SHAPE of the organism you buried (for example a shell or a bone).'
When a footprint is fossilised via the toggle: 'This is a trace fossil — evidence of activity — different from a body fossil like a shell or bone.'
activities.rationale: Acting out each stage and controlling time is intended to make both big ideas (quick burial, vast time) concrete, and the burial-choice branch addresses the 'any dead thing becomes a fossil' and 'fossils form quickly' misconceptions. The body-vs-trace toggle covers the required examples. The burial choice, draggable layers, and time slider are illustrative interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Fossilisation requires rapid burial in sediment and occurs over very long time; body fossils preserve shape via mineralisation while trace fossils record activity (tracks, imprints); fossils occur mainly in sedimentary rock.
DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils describe in simple terms how fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock.
learnerActions: Place a dead organism (for example a shell or a small animal) on an ancient seabed.
Face a choice: bury it now or wait — if you wait too long, scavengers, decay and moving water can break up and scatter it so nothing is left to become a fossil; choose to bury it quickly.
Drag layer after layer of sediment on top of the buried organism.
Move a time slider to sweep across a very long time (millions of years) and watch soft mud compress and harden into rock while the organism's shape is preserved in stone.
Dig down and lift out the finished fossil.
Use a toggle to make a trace fossil instead: leave a footprint in the mud and fossilise that.
activities.intendedInsight: Fossilisation is a time-ordered process with a hidden mechanism; quick burial is essential (waiting too long usually means the remains are rotted, broken up or scattered before they can be preserved) and the process takes an unimaginably long time. The shape is preserved in rock rather than the unchanged original surviving.

activities.title: Sequence and sort the fossil facts
feedback: If stages are out of order, highlight that burial must come before layers build up and before rock forms.
If a footprint is sorted as a body fossil, clarify it records activity, not the organism's body, so it is a trace fossil.
If 'days' or 'years' is chosen for timescale, restate that fossilisation takes a very long time — millions of years.
activities.rationale: Sequencing and classifying give checkable practice of the standard's described steps and examples. Recognition-and-ordering tasks check understanding but do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing their own explanation; pair with retelling.
sourceClaims: Fossilisation requires rapid burial in sediment and occurs over very long time; body fossils preserve shape via mineralisation while trace fossils record activity (tracks, imprints); fossils occur mainly in sedimentary rock.
learnerActions: Put the five fossilisation stages in order: organism dies → buried quickly in mud/sand → layers build up and press down → sediment turns to rock over millions of years (shape preserved) → rock exposed and fossil found.
Sort example cards into body fossils (shell, bone) versus trace fossils (footprint, imprint).
Answer how long fossils take to form: days, years, or millions of years (millions of years).
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the ordered sequence, the body-vs-trace distinction, and the vast timescale.

activities.title: Retell the fossil story and explain the conditions
feedback: If the learner says it's the 'very same shell unchanged', explain the shape is preserved but the material is often replaced and turned to rock over time.
If the learner implies all dead things fossilise, note fossils are rare — they need quick burial in the right conditions; most things rot away.
If the timescale is left out, prompt for how long it takes (millions of years).
activities.rationale: Spoken or written retelling requires the learner to construct the explanation rather than recognise it, matching the standard's 'describe in simple terms' goal and surfacing the key misconceptions. The park-leaves prompt probes the rarity/conditions idea.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils describe in simple terms how fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock.

Fossilisation requires rapid burial in sediment and occurs over very long time; body fossils preserve shape via mineralisation while trace fossils record activity (tracks, imprints); fossils occur mainly in sedimentary rock.
learnerActions: In your own words, retell the fossil-formation sequence in order, from the organism dying to the fossil being found.
Explain why most dead things — like leaves that fall in a park every autumn — do NOT become fossils.
State what has to happen to the dead animal or plant first, before it can become a fossil.
Describe whether a shell fossil found in rock is the unchanged original shell or something else, and how a shell ended up inside rock.
activities.intendedInsight: A full explanation names burial in sediment, layers building up, sediment turning to rock over millions of years with the shape preserved, and why fossilisation is rare.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal cross-section of the stages
feedback: Each revealed caption names the stage (burial, layering, compression, rock formation, exposure).
The lift-the-flap reinforces that fast burial protects the body from rotting and scattering.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal cross-section presents the stage sequence and vocabulary clearly. It presents the process rather than letting the learner control burial and time, so it works best as a reference or scaffold alongside the driveable simulation and retelling.
sourceClaims: Fossilisation requires rapid burial in sediment and occurs over very long time; body fossils preserve shape via mineralisation while trace fossils record activity (tracks, imprints); fossils occur mainly in sedimentary rock.
learnerActions: Tap each layer/stage of a layered cross-section scene to reveal a caption explaining what is happening at that step.
Open a lift-the-flap labelled 'Why must it be buried quickly?' and read the explanation.
activities.intendedInsight: The sequence and vocabulary of fossil formation, presented as a labelled cross-section through the sediment layers.

activities.title: Plaster cast of a shell (hands-on)
feedback: Discuss: the plaster isn't the shell, but it kept its shape — like how rock keeps a fossil's shape even when the original material changes.
Note the limits: this takes minutes, while real fossilisation takes millions of years and happens inside hardening sediment, not plaster.
activities.rationale: A physical cast/mould makes preservation-of-shape tangible and is intended to target the 'fossil is the unchanged original' misconception. It is an analogy with important differences (timescale, materials), so name those limits explicitly.
sourceClaims: Fossilisation requires rapid burial in sediment and occurs over very long time; body fossils preserve shape via mineralisation while trace fossils record activity (tracks, imprints); fossils occur mainly in sedimentary rock.
learnerActions: Press a shell firmly into clay or plasticine to leave a clear imprint, then remove the shell.
Pour plaster into the imprint and let it set.
Lift out the plaster and compare its shape to the original shell.
activities.intendedInsight: The surrounding material can keep the SHAPE of an object even after the original is gone — a concrete analogy for how rock preserves a fossil's shape.

activities.title: Ask the palaeontologist (optional extension)
feedback: Responses should connect back to the ordered process and emphasise that most dead things rot away before they can fossilise.
activities.rationale: An expert Q&A can field a curious child's questions and may reinforce the rarity/conditions idea. Use it as a supplement because an open question-and-answer format is not structured to ensure the learner systematically works through or produces the full ordered sequence themselves; use it after the process is established.
learnerActions: Ask an in-role palaeontologist 'why/how' questions, such as 'Why don't most animals become fossils?' or 'How did this particular fossil form?'
Use the answers to deepen your understanding of the conditions needed for fossilisation.
activities.intendedInsight: Fossils are rare and depend on specific conditions (quick burial, the right environment); curiosity-driven questions can deepen the conditions idea.

activities.title: 3D excavation (optional engagement extra)
feedback: Connect the dig back to the process: 'This fossil formed through burial and millions of years before it could be dug out.'
activities.rationale: A 3D excavation may add excavation realism and engagement. The core learning target is the process sequence and timescale rather than spatial handling, so treat this as an engaging extra, not the central mechanism.
learnerActions: After a fossil has formed, rotate the rock and carefully extract the fossil from it in a 3D dig.
Observe how the fossil sits embedded in the surrounding rock.
activities.intendedInsight: Fossils are embedded in rock and uncovered by excavation; this adds realism to the 'exposed and found' stage.

constraints: Teach fossilisation as an ORDERED sequence (die → bury quickly → layers build and compress → turn to rock over millions of years with shape preserved → exposed/found) and have children retell it in order.
Foreground the two big ideas: quick burial before decay, and immense time (millions of years).
Distinguish body fossils (shape preserved: shells, bones) from trace fossils (footprints, imprints) with examples.
Link to prior learning — fossils form mainly in sedimentary rock, and only once-living things fossilise.

Address common misconceptions explicitly: the fossil is not the unchanged original (material is often replaced and the shape preserved in rock); fossilisation is slow, not quick; most dead things do NOT fossilise; fossils are not found in any rock; a footprint IS a fossil (trace fossil); dinosaurs are one example, not the whole concept.
Keep feedback consistent with whatever specimen the learner actually buries in the simulation (a generic organism, or a named shell) rather than switching between them.
The plaster-cast activity is an analogy with important limits: it takes minutes (not millions of years) and uses plaster (not hardening sediment); state these differences.
Sequencing, sorting, and multiple-choice tasks check understanding but do not require the learner to construct their own explanation; pair them with spoken or written retelling.

The tap-to-reveal cross-section, 3D excavation, and expert Q&A are scaffolds/supplements that present or deepen the process but do not let the learner drive burial and time; keep a driveable process and retelling as the core. They are not incapable of conveying content — they simply do not, in these formats, require the learner to drive or produce the full ordered sequence.
Optional interaction examples (burial-now-vs-wait choice, draggable layers, time slider, lift-the-flap, toggle to trace fossil) make the mechanism concrete but are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Both sources are marked verified:false in the row; treat the DfE standard wording and the NHM fossilisation description accordingly.

The simulation originally described the body 'mineralising into stone'; the sources note mineralisation/replacement preserves shape. Child-level framing is kept ('the shape is kept in rock, the material is often slowly replaced by minerals') and detailed mechanism is not overstated for ages 7–8.

'Fossilisation takes millions of years' is retained as a single timescale for age-appropriateness and source consistency; real timescales vary and can be shorter. This simplification is deliberate, not independently verified, and the 'days/years/millions' question keeps 'years' only as a misconception distractor, not as a hidden correct answer.
Simulation feedback refers to the organism the learner actually buried (with a shell-or-bone example) rather than silently assuming a shell.

The 'made by people' misconception noted in the source's 'gap' response level is only indirectly addressed through the plaster-cast analogy ('the plaster isn't the shell'); no dedicated activity targets it.

Fit rankings, product/catalog terminology, and quiz-step vocabulary from the source have been removed; comparative/necessity framing (e.g. simulation 'perfect', 3D 'adds nothing', conversation 'can't SHOW the process') has been softened to scoped affordance limits rather than universal claims about what a medium can or cannot teach.

probeDeeper: Why don't the leaves that fall in a park every autumn turn into fossils?
About how long does it take for a fossil to form — days, years, or millions of years?
What has to happen to the dead animal or plant first, before it can become a fossil?
assess.correctAnswer: It's usually not the unchanged original. The shell was buried in mud or sand, more layers piled on top, and over millions of years the sediment turned to rock while the shell's shape was preserved (often the material is slowly replaced by minerals). So the rock kept the SHAPE of the shell over a very long time.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A fossil is just the actual original bone or shell, unchanged'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The shape is preserved but the material is often replaced and turned to rock over time.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's the very same shell, exactly as it was.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats the fossil as the untouched original object

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Fossils form quickly — you could make one in a few years'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Emphasise millions of years of slow burial and layering.
errorPatterns.distractor: The shell turned into a fossil in just a few years.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: no sense of the huge timescale

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Any dead thing always becomes a fossil'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fossils are rare — they need quick burial in the right conditions; most things rot away.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: thinks fossilisation is guaranteed for everything that dies

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the fossil is the unchanged original, or that it formed quickly or was made by people.
responseLevels.full: Describes burial in sediment, layers building up, sediment turning to rock over millions of years with the organism's shape preserved, and explains why most dead things don't fossilise.
responseLevels.partial: Knows fossils are old and found in rock but leaves out burial, the long timescale, or that the shape is preserved as sediment turns to rock.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A fossil of a shell is found inside solid rock. Is that the actual original shell that was there millions of years ago, or something else? And how did a shell end up inside rock in the first place?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the fossil is simply the original object sitting in rock, or that it formed quickly, differs from one who describes burial, a very long timescale, and preservation of the shape.
